story: Most of the park lies on the Northern Boreal Plains, flat and poorly drained, between about 210 and 300 metres above sea level. Beneath the glacial deposits is Devonian sedimentary rock — gypsum, salt, dolomite and limestone — and because it is porous and soluble, water here drains downwards rather than across the land. That has made one of the finest gypsum karst landscapes in North America: sinkholes, underground streams and saline springs. Where the springs reach the surface they leave white salt mounds and crusts across the Salt Plains, with salt-tolerant plants growing around them.

In the south-east, the Peace, Athabasca and Birch rivers meet at the western end of Lake Athabasca to form the Peace-Athabasca Delta, 3,900 square kilometres of channels, lakes, marshes and sedge meadow, 80 per cent of it inside the park. It is one of the largest inland freshwater deltas in the world, with 45 kinds of mammal, 214 of birds and 20 of fish, and waterfowl from all four North American flyways stop here. Its channels can flow either way: when an ice jam on the Peace River backs water up, it pours south into the delta and refills the perched basins that only floods can reach. Such floods have become rarer in recent decades.

The park was created in 1922 to protect the last free-roaming bison of the region, and extended south of the Peace River in 1926 after plains bison shipped north from Buffalo National Park in Alberta crossed the river. Today around 3,000 wood bison live here, the largest free-roaming, self-regulating herd of its kind in the world, still hunted by wolves as they always have been. In a remote maze of shallow ponds in the north of the park nests the last natural wild flock of whooping cranes, North America's tallest bird; it migrates 4,000 kilometres each way to the Texas coast and numbered an estimated 505 birds in 2018, up from near-extinction in the 1940s.

Indigenous people have lived in this country for more than 8,000 years, and the Cree, Dene and Métis communities around the park still hunt, fish and trap in it. The park's founding treated that use as a privilege granted to some families and not others, which divided communities. Court rulings changed that: since 2003 Parks Canada has respected the asserted Métis right to hunt, and the Supreme Court's 2005 Mikisew Cree decision recognised the Treaty 8 right to harvest here. The park is now managed with eleven Indigenous partners, and in 1983 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
howItWorks: Wood Buffalo is open all year, but visitor services run from May to October and the park's fee list has no admission charge: you pay for campsites, backcountry nights, fishing permits and rentals. Elsewhere in the Parks Canada system, a Discovery Pass gives twelve months' admission at more than 80 places and is sold at Wood Buffalo; in 2026 it costs $83.50 for an adult, $71.50 for a senior and $167.50 for a family or group of up to seven in one vehicle. Youth 17 and under have been admitted free at all Parks Canada places since 2018, and Parks Canada last adjusted its fees on 1 January 2026.

Pine Lake Campground has 18 unserviced sites, open from the Victoria Day weekend to 30 September; ten of them, and the Kettle Point group camp, are booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service, online or at 1-877-737-3783, and the rest are first come, first served with a self-registration permit at the kiosk. Backcountry camping is random — there are no designated sites — and needs a permit from the visitor centre in Fort Smith or Fort Chipewyan, or by phone on 867-872-7960. Camp at least 50 metres from water, 100 metres from any road or trail and 1 kilometre from trailheads and day-use areas. Checking out with staff when you return is optional, but if you choose to and do not come back on time, Parks Canada starts a search. After the 2023 fires, permits were issued only for itineraries outside recently burned areas, and fire-related closures may still apply.

The Canada National Parks Act makes it illegal to feed wildlife, directly or by leaving food or garbage out. Parks Canada asks visitors here to stay at least 30 metres from moose and 100 metres from bears, wolves and bison, to slow down and stay in the car when animals are beside the road, and to keep dogs on a leash at all times. The BARE campsite policy applies at Pine Lake: keep anything with a scent locked away. Recreational drones are prohibited, with fines of up to $25,000. Fishing needs a national park fishing permit, from Victoria Day to 15 October, and subsistence harvesting by Treaty 8 First Nations and Métis continues in the park.

sightNotes.poi-ca-wood-buffalo-pine-lake: An aquamarine sinkhole lake 60 km south of Fort Smith, with a sandy beach, the park's campground, rental cabins, canoe launch and the Dark Sky Circle.
sightNotes.poi-ca-wood-buffalo-salt-river-day-use-a: Picnic ground 24 km south of Fort Smith above the Salt River, with the Dëldël Kué shelter, trailheads and red-sided garter snakes emerging in late April and May.
sightNotes.poi-ca-wood-buffalo-salt-river-meadows-l: A bench and lookout on the 2.2-kilometre loop through wildflower meadows beside a saline stream, starting across the road from the Salt River day-use area.
sightNotes.poi-ca-wood-buffalo-lane-lake: A lake south of Pine Lake at the end of the 6.5-kilometre Lane Lake Trail. The trail was closed in 2026 after the 2023 fires; check first.
sightNotes.poi-ca-wood-buffalo-sweetgrass-landing: On the Peace River, the start of the 14-kilometre walk to Sweetgrass Station, a 1950s–70s bison management station with corrals and heritage buildings in the delta meadows.
sightNotes.poi-ca-wood-buffalo-lake-claire: One of the major lakes of the Peace-Athabasca Delta, which rises when floods on the Peace and Athabasca rivers back water into the delta.
sightNotes.poi-ca-wood-buffalo-worlds-largest-beave: A dam about 775 metres long across its face, visible from space, holding back run-off from the Birch Mountains. No road or trail: days of trekking or a chartered sightseeing tour.

chronology.text: Archaeological evidence shows Indigenous people living in the region by this time.
Fur traders arrive in the region.
Wood Buffalo National Park is established north of the Peace River to protect the free-roaming bison of the area.
The park is extended south of the Peace River into the Peace-Athabasca Delta, to protect plains bison shipped north that had crossed the river.
Sweetgrass Station in the delta operates as a bison management station.
The Peace-Athabasca Delta and the whooping crane nesting area are designated Ramsar wetlands of international importance.
UNESCO inscribes Wood Buffalo as Canada's eighth World Heritage Site.
The Supreme Court's Mikisew Cree decision recognises the Treaty 8 right to hunt, fish and trap in the park, ending the old permit system.
On 28 June the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada designates the park the world's largest Dark Sky Preserve.
Canada and its partners release an action plan for the World Heritage Site, focused on the Peace-Athabasca Delta.
Wildfires burn 929,521 hectares in the park, about a fifth of it, and affect every recreational trail.

safety: Bison are big and fast, often on or beside the roads, and most aggressive in the rut from late July to September. Stay at least 100 metres away, drive slowly and remain in your vehicle.
Cell coverage is unreliable everywhere in the park. Carry a satellite messenger or phone, and know that Pine Lake Campground has an emergency radio-phone. Park emergencies: 1-877-852-3100.
In areas burned in 2023, fire-weakened trees can fall without warning and ash pits can burn or injure you. Respect all closures and report fires or smoke to 867-621-0136.
Pine Lake drops off quickly and has no lifeguards; water from the lake must be filtered or treated before drinking. Winter temperatures can reach −40°C, and the winter road needs full preparation.
regulations: Never feed wildlife or leave food, coolers or garbage unattended; the BARE campsite policy applies at Pine Lake.
Dogs must be on a leash at all times.
Recreational drones are prohibited, with fines of up to $25,000.
Backcountry campers need a permit and must camp at least 50 metres from water, 100 metres from roads and trails and 1 kilometre from trailheads and day-use areas.
Fishing needs a national park fishing permit; walleye must be longer than 43 centimetres, and daily limits apply.

weather: Summers, June to August, are mostly warm and dry, from about 10°C to 30°C, with 14 to 19 hours of daylight and the highest wildfire risk. September and October are cool, windy and dry, between 4°C and 20°C, with bright autumn colour, fewer insects and the first snow by the end of October; freeze-up usually comes in late October or early November. Winter, November to April, is cold, dry and sunny under deep snow, with temperatures that can reach −40°C in January and February. Spring break-up usually begins around the end of April or early May. Pine Lake is ice-free by mid to late June and warm enough for swimming from July into early September.
directions: Fort Smith, the park's headquarters, is reached year-round by road. From Yellowknife take Highway 3 south, then Highways 1, 2 and 5; from Edmonton drive north to High Level, then Highway 35 to the territorial border, the Mackenzie Highway to Enterprise, and Highways 2 and 5, which run 264 kilometres through the park to Fort Smith. Highway 5 is mostly hard-packed gravel. Pine Lake Road leads south from Fort Smith to the Salt River Day Use Area and Pine Lake. There is no all-weather road to Fort Chipewyan; Northwestern Air Lease flies to Fort Smith and Fort Chipewyan from Edmonton and Yellowknife, and in winter a road over snow and ice may link Fort Smith, Fort Chipewyan and Fort McMurray for about three months.
